name: GO Classes CS Test Series 2025 | Discrete Mathematics | Topic wise Test 4

question.text: Consider the set of $4$-digit positive integers. How many of them have their digits in strictly increasing order? (i.e. $1234, 2578$ etc)
Consider the set $\text{X} = \{2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9\},$ which contains $8$ elements. How many subsets of $\text{X}$ have at least one prime number?

Let the recurrence for the number of sequences of length $n$ containing digits from $\{0, 1, \dots, 6 \},$ which do not have consecutive even digits be $\text{T}(n).$

For instance$, 05565301$ is a sequence of length 8 containing digits from $\{0, 1, \dots, 6 \},$ which do not have consecutive even digits.

We can see that $\text{T}_{1} = 7, \text{T}_{2} = 33,$ which are the initial conditions of the recurrence $\text{T}(n).$

For $n \geq 3, \text{T}(n) = x\text{T}_{n-1} + y\text{T}_{n-2}$

Then what is $x+y?$

Let $\text{S}$ be a set consisting of $10$ elements. We want to count all the ways to form an unordered pair $\{\text{A, B}\}$ of disjoint subsets of $\text{S i.e. A} \subseteq \text{S, B} \subseteq \text{S},$ and $\text{A, B}$ are disjoint sets. How many ways are there?

Note that we will consider $\{\text{X, X}\}$ also as an unordered pair. Also, $\{\text{X, Y}\} = \{\text{Y, X}\}.$

Let $n \in \mathbf{N}$ be a natural number and let $\text{X} \subseteq \mathbf{N}$ be a subset with $n + 1$ elements.

Then which of the following is/are necessarily true ?

  1. there exist two distinct natural numbers $x, y \in \text{X}$ such that $x-y$ is divisible by $n.$
  2. there exist two distinct natural numbers $x, y \in \text{X}$ such that both $x, y$ are divisible by $n.$
  3. there exist two distinct natural numbers $x, y \in \text{X}$ such that $x + y$ is divisible by $n.$
  4. there exist two distinct natural numbers $x, y \in \text{X}$ such that $xy$ is divisible by $n.$

Let $0 \leq \text{S(0)} \leq \text{T(0)},$ and suppose we have the recurrences

  • $\text{S}(n + 1) = a\text{S}(n) + f(n)$
  • $\text{T}(n + 1) = b\text{T}(n) + g(n),$

where $0 \leq a \leq b$ and $0 \leq f(n) \leq g(n)$ for all $n \in \mathbf{N}.$

Which of the following is/are necessarily true ?

  1. $\text{S}(n) \leq \text{T}(n)$ for all $n \in \mathbf{N}.$
  2. $\text{T}(n) \leq \text{S}(n)$ for all $n \in \mathbf{N}.$
  3. $\text{T}(n) < \text{S}(n)$ for some $n \in \mathbf{N}.$
  4. $0 \leq \text{S}(n) \leq \text{T}(n)$ for all $n \in \mathbf{N}.$

What is the coefficient of $x^{5}$ in the power series expansion of the following function?

$$\frac{1+7x}{(1-x)(1-5x)}$$

A student is given an exam consisting of $8$ essay questions divided into $4$ groups of $2$ questions each. The student is required to select a set of $6$ questions to answer, including at least $1$ question from each of the $4$ groups. How many sets of questions satisfy this requirement?

Count the number of ways to place the numbers $1, 2, \dots, 10$ (all of them) on the left and bottom side of the square below (below gray squares), such that for each gray box, the number on its left is smaller than the number below it.

How many integer solutions does the equation

$$
x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4=15
$$
have, if we require that $x_1 \geq 2, x_2 \geq 3, x_3 \geq 10$ and $x_4 \geq-3?$

Consider the set $\text{X} = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ and $\text{Y} = \{a, b, c, d, e, f\}.$ How many one-to-one functions $\text{F}$ are there from $\text{X}$ to $\text{Y}$ so that $\text{F(1)}$ is not a vowel?

Let $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots$ be a sequence with generating function $G(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n x^n$, and let $b_0, b_1, b_2, \ldots$ be the sequence whose generating function is $F(x) = G(3x^{2}).$

  • Let $b_{11} = m.a_{11}$
  • Let $b_{20} = p.a_{10}$

What is $m+p?$
How many ways are there to arrange the $12$ letters of $\text{AAABBBBCCCCC}$ without having two $\text{Cs}$ together?

There are five people of different heights. In how many ways can they stand in a line, so there are no $3$ consecutive people with increasing height(from left to right)? (Hint: May Try Inclusion-Exclusion Principle)

How many words can be formed by re-arranging the letters of the word $\text{“PROBLEMS”}$ such that $\text{P}$ and $\text{S}$ occupy the first and last position respectively? (Note: The words thus formed need not be meaningful)
